title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: Bernstein and Keay address different questions
text:
Bernstein and Keay address different questions


August 31 · Bernstein
How are trade rules created, contested, evaded, and changed?
Restricted access · illicit commerce · domestic conflict · coercion

September 2 · Keay
What kind of organization made this trade possible?
Risk · chartered monopoly · armed commerce · delegated authority


Today we study political conflict over trade. Wednesday we dive into corporate power.


Timing: 0–3 minutes. Explain the fixed reading sequence. Bernstein begins with the mature political economy of long-distance trade: restricted access, monopoly, illicit commerce, distributional conflict, coercion, and changing rules. Keay then steps back to explain the organizational form that made such trade possible and accumulated quasi-state powers. Do not resolve the EIC organizational puzzle today.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: Your IB Voice
text:
Your IB Voice


Question


Britain and China had traded at Canton for over a century without war. In 1839 they went to war. What changed? Defend your answer with evidence from the reading.



10 minutes · Individual · Notes allowed · No internet or LLMs


Timing: 3–13 minutes. Ask students to choose a primary explanation and defend it with chapter evidence. The purpose is to generate competing hypotheses before the lecture reconstructs the sequence. Do not resolve the question. Strongest answer is roughly: enforcement became urgent for Beijing at the same moment restraint disappeared on the British side, and the confiscation turned a smuggling dispute into a Crown liability.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: Hypotheses
text:
Hypotheses

What explains the war?


Take each one: was it also true in 1780?


Timing: MM–MM minutes.
Take four or five answers and write each on the board as a short phrase. Do not sort or group them. Then advance to reveal the second question and work down the board one hypothesis at a time. Anything true in 1780 has a timing problem the student needs to solve; anything that is not is a candidate cause, so ask that student what set it off when it did. Leave the board list standing for the rest of class.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: Canton permitted trade on Qing terms
text:
Canton permitted trade on Qing terms





The Qing state confined Western foreign trade to Canton and licensed Chinese hongs (merchant houses).

The aim was to keep silver at home and foreign influence out.

Qing authorities used the Canton system to control the terms of foreign trade.



William Daniell, View of the Canton Factories, 1805–06 · Wikimedia Commons, public domain


Timing: 18–22 minutes. Define the Canton System through three controls: where foreigners could trade, through whom, and under what conditions. Explain that concern about silver outflows is recognizably mercantilist, while the broader objective is sovereignty: obtain gains from trade while limiting foreign penetration, dependence, and political influence.
[Sources] - William J. Bernstein, A Splendid Exchange, Chapter 11, pp. 284–287. - William Daniell, View of the Canton Factories, 1805–06, Wikimedia Commons, public domain.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: Britain paid for tea with silver
text:
Britain paid for tea with silver



≈90%


of the value Britain sent to China was bullion


In 1751, Britain sent £119,000 in silver and £10,842 in merchandise.
Britain bought tea and silk. China bought little that Britain made.


The imbalance created pressure to find something China would buy.


Timing: 22–25 minutes. Bernstein reports that roughly 90 percent of the value of eighteenth-century British exports to China was bullion and provides the 1751 example. Ask whether the imbalance itself necessarily causes conflict or becomes dangerous through the responses it induces.
[Source] - Bernstein, Chapter 11, pp. 286–287.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: Mercantilism linked commerce to national power
text:
Mercantilism linked commerce to national power
State power: Commerce should strengthen the state
Bullion: Gold and silver supported public credit, military spending, and political power
Trade balance: Export surpluses brought bullion into the country
Empire: Colonies and chartered companies like EIC secured supplies, markets, shipping

Britain bought Chinese goods with silver while China bought little British merchandise. Mercantilists saw the outflow as a loss of national wealth and power.


Timing: 18–21 minutes. Define mercantilism as a view of commerce shaped by national power and rivalry. Bullion mattered because it supported public credit, military spending, and the fiscal capacity of the state. Mercantilists did not oppose all imports. Imports that strengthened national production or power could be valuable. Their concerns were dependency, bullion loss, and whether trade strengthened another state more than their own. Use this framework to explain why Britain’s persistent silver outflow to China appeared to require a solution.
[Sources] - William J. Bernstein, A Splendid Exchange, Chapter 11, pp. 284–287. - Lars Magnusson, The Political Economy of Mercantilism (Routledge, 2015). - Francis Swaine, An East Indiaman in Stays, c. 1780, Royal Museums Greenwich / Wikimedia Commons, public domain.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: From cotton to opium
text:
From cotton to opium





The EIC grew and auctioned opium in India. Private traders carried it into China.


The increased imports led to silver outflows from China, which they tried to halt



Opium factory at Patna, c. 1851 · Wikimedia Commons, public domain


Timing: 25–30 minutes. Explain the triangle briefly before the opium step: the EIC’s position in Bengal gave it Indian cotton, which China bought, so Britain routed trade through India to cover its bilateral imbalance with China; when Chinese demand for Indian cotton weakened, the commercial search continued and opium took cotton’s place. Then distinguish the Company’s legal position in India from the private traders’ illicit entry into China. The analytical point is strategic response: commercial and political actors chose an organizational solution to the imbalance.
[Sources] - Bernstein, Chapter 11, pp. 287–290. - Opium factory at Patna, c. 1851, Wikimedia Commons, public domain.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: Barriers created rents and rewarded evasion
text:
Barriers created rents and rewarded evasion


Regulation redirected commerce through smugglers and intermediaries.


Timing: 30–33 minutes. Define rents as returns created by restricted access or an artificial price wedge. Chinese controls did not remove demand for market access; they encouraged organizational separation, intermediaries, smuggling, and illicit commerce. Save contemporary analogies for the end.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: Production and finance kept the EIC at the center
text:
Production and finance kept the EIC at the center




The Company auctioned opium in India.
Private traders sold it in China for silver.
The silver bought Company bills.
EIC silver bought tea.

Infrastructural power: the EIC never carried opium into China, yet every stage of the trade ran through it.



The Opium Trade in China, 1833–1839 · MIT Visualizing Cultures


Timing: 33–37 minutes. Walk through the four steps of the circuit on the slide. Then ask the question the slide implies: how did the EIC shape an illegal trade that private merchants conducted? Introduce “infrastructural power”: the capacity to shape production, finance, and exchange without directing every transaction. Pose the organizational puzzle but do not solve it. Keay explains the origins of this capacity on September 2.
[Sources] - Bernstein, Chapter 11, pp. 287–291. - MIT Visualizing Cultures, The Opium Trade in China, 1833–1839.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: Lin Zexu turned tension into crisis
text:
Lin Zexu turned tension into crisis



40,000


chests of opium a year by the late 1830s, four times the 1825 level



In 1839, Commissioner Lin detained foreign merchants and destroyed more than 20,000 chests of opium.

To the Qing court, this was enforcement of Chinese law and sovereignty.
To British merchants, it was an attack on property and commerce.


Timing: 37–42 minutes. Start with the numbers: the EIC lost its China monopoly in 1834, private firms such as Jardine Matheson combined the country trade with the tea trade, and Bernstein reports growth from roughly 10,000 to 40,000 chests. Removing one monopoly did not make the trading system lawful or apolitical. Lin’s intervention followed arrests of local smugglers and mounting social and fiscal consequences. Ask students to give the strongest account of each interpretation. The enforcement shock is endogenous: it arose from consequences produced by the trading regime itself.
[Source] - Bernstein, Chapter 11, pp. 290–297.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: Commercial interests mobilized military power
text:
Commercial interests mobilized military power





Merchants lobbied London for compensation and wider access. The government sent warships.


Britain’s use of military force to expand market access led to interstate conflict: the Opium War.



E. Duncan, The Nemesis Destroying Chinese War Junks, 1843 · National Maritime Museum / MIT Visualizing Cultures


Timing: 42–45 minutes. Jardine and other merchants pressed the British cabinet for a favorable treaty backed by naval force. The Nemesis was built for the EIC and designed for shallow Chinese waters. Emphasize the political translation from commercial grievance to state coercion.
[Sources] - Bernstein, Chapter 11, pp. 297–302. - E. Duncan, The Nemesis Destroying Chinese War Junks, 1843, National Maritime Museum / MIT Visualizing Cultures.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: The Treaty of Nanking rewrote the rules of trade
text:
The Treaty of Nanking rewrote the rules of trade


Indemnity · Hong Kong · five treaty ports · end of the hong monopoly · (eventually) low tariffs


John Platt and John Burnet, The Signing of the Treaty of Nanking, 1846 · Anne S. K. Brown Military Collection / Wikimedia Commons, public domain


Timing: 45–48 minutes. No provision legalized opium. The treaty nevertheless changed market access, tariff authority, and territorial control; subsequent agreements expanded British privileges. Return briefly to the opening hypotheses: the imbalance was a pressure, restrictions shaped the response, commercial interests mobilized, and coercive state power changed the rules.
[Sources] - Bernstein, Chapter 11, pp. 302–304. - John Platt and John Burnet, The Signing of the Treaty of Nanking, 1846, Anne S. K. Brown Military Collection / Wikimedia Commons, public domain.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: The Long Path to More Open Trade
text:
The Long Path to More Open Trade


Sovereignty → trade restrictions → rents → circumvention


Crackdown → interstate conflict → forced rule change


Responses to the trade imbalance transformed commercial tensions into interstate conflict.


Timing: 48–51 minutes. Abstract the mechanism only after reconstructing the case. This is one pathway: controlled access generates circumvention; growing consequences provoke enforcement; enforcement triggers interstate conflict; power then produces forced rule change.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: What did the Corn Laws actually do?
text:
What did the Corn Laws actually do?





Who is protected when wheat prices fall below 63 shillings? Who pays?



Bernstein, A Splendid Exchange, Chapter 11, Table 11-1


Timing: 51–54 minutes. Ask students to read the schedule before explaining it. When the domestic wheat price fell below 63 shillings, the 24.25-shilling import levy made foreign grain much more expensive. The rule protected domestic landowners and grain prices while raising food costs for consumers. Use their answers to introduce the distributional positions on the next slide.
[Source] - William J. Bernstein, A Splendid Exchange, Chapter 11, Table 11-1.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: Free-trade ideas became a political program
text:
Free-trade ideas became a political program

Smith and Ricardo showed that protection raised costs and blocked gains from trade. Cobden’s League organized that argument into a campaign for repeal.

The League turned an abstract economic argument into policy.


Timing: 54–58 minutes. Comparative advantage appears here as part of the ideas component. Smith and Ricardo supplied a framework. Cobden and the Anti-Corn Law League converted it into a campaign. Landowner interests and parliamentary influence kept repeal blocked until 1845.
[Source] - Bernstein, Chapter 11, pp. 305–312.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: Prepare a 30-second statement for the public hearing
text:
Prepare a 30-second statement for the public hearing


5 minutes · Individual · Notes permitted


Maintain, modify, or repeal? Consider your two strongest arguments, who gains and who loses, and the strongest argument against your position.


Timing: 58–65 minutes. Physically divide the room into three sides. Assign students rather than allowing self-selection if one side is sparse. They are not formal groups: every student prepares an individual argument and may be called on. Establish the material stakes as you assign sides: landowners held concentrated interests and disproportionate institutional influence, industrialists were a rising economic constituency, and urban workers and consumers bore higher food costs without equivalent political power. Then circulate and press students to distinguish material interests, public arguments, and political leverage. Do not mention the famine.
[Source] - Bernstein, Chapter 11, pp. 305–312.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: Public hearing
text:
Public hearing

Should Britain maintain, modify, or repeal the Corn Laws?


We will hear from each side. Listen for interests, expected winners and losers, political influence, and ideas.


Timing: 65–74 minutes. Cold-call multiple students from each side for short testimony and rebuttal. On the board, sort claims under material interests, winners and losers, political influence, and arguments or ideas. Surface the stable protectionist equilibrium without yet naming shocks as the lesson.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: Round 2
text:
Round 2

Does the shock change your position?

If yes, what changed in your reasoning? If no, how do you defend the existing policy now?

2 minutes · Individual reconsideration


Timing: 75–80 minutes. Give students two minutes, then take brief testimony from each side. Ask whether the shock changed material interests, moral and political costs, expectations about governing survival, or the viability of the existing coalition.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: The famine raised the political cost of protection
text:
The famine raised the political cost of protection

Landowners gained from protection and dominated Parliament. But repeal was a known possibility already circulating in political debate.

The crisis fractured the governing coalition and made repeal possible.


Timing: 80–83 minutes. Interests and institutions remained in place. The shock raised the political cost of protection, strengthened an available policy alternative, and enabled political realignment under Peel.
[Source] - Bernstein, Chapter 11, pp. 310–312.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: Two pathways made trade rules unstable
text:
Two pathways made trade rules unstable


China
Restrictions
→ circumvention
→ crackdown
→ interstate conflict
→ forced rule change

Corn Laws
Distributional conflict
→ durable coalition
→ external shock
→ political realignment
→ liberalization


Rules create rents, coalitions defend them, institutions sustain them, and ideas plus shocks change them.


Timing: 83–87 minutes. Do not force the cases into one identical model. China’s enforcement shock emerged from the consequences of the trade regime and led to coercive interstate change. The famine was an external shock that changed domestic coalition politics. Then read the key line as the conceptual payoff: interests supply preferences; institutions weight those preferences; ideas supply interpretations and alternatives; shocks change the political costs and coalition possibilities. Ask students to name the actor, institution, idea, and destabilizing event in each case. Neither markets nor policy changes are self-executing, and repeal was political change, not the automatic implementation of economic truth.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: The same mechanisms shape international business today
text:
The same mechanisms shape international business today







18th and 19th Centuries
International business today




Mercantilism and controlled access
Economic security and strategic sovereignty


Smuggling and intermediaries
Transshipment and sanctions evasion


EIC production and financial infrastructure
Big Tech dominance


Corn Law coalition and famine
Sectoral lobbying and crisis-driven realignment




When states constrain globalization, firms reorganize trade around the new limits.


Timing: 87–89 minutes. Keep the analogies brief. The claim is not that history repeats or that the cases are equivalent. The recurring mechanisms are controlled access, rents, circumvention, infrastructural power, distributional coalitions, and shock-driven realignment.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: The EIC puzzle remains
text:
The EIC puzzle remains

What kind of company could organize trade, finance, coercion, and political authority across continents?


On Wednesday we ask why long-distance trade required a chartered company and how that company acquired such immense power.


Timing: 89–90 minutes. Return to the unresolved EIC puzzle. Monday established the Company’s infrastructural capacity. Keay explains how long-distance risk and organizational problems produced the chartered-company form, and how capabilities created for commerce became foundations of political power and empire.

title: Shipping Containers and Global Supply Chains
section: Module 3: what makes international (“cross-border”) business costly?
text:
Module 3: what makes international (“cross-border”) business costly?



Geographic friction
Today: containerization
Freight · time · handling · coordination


Border friction
Next: currencies · jurisdictions · trade rules
Exchange rates · legal systems · trade policy · political risk


Kees Torn / Wikimedia Commons · U.S. Customs and Border Protection


Timing: 0-3. Module map: distance today, currencies tomorrow, jurisdictions 14th, trade rules 16th.

title: Shipping Containers and Global Supply Chains
section: Your IB Voice
text:
Your IB Voice


Question


Levinson says the container’s value lies in how it is used. What exactly did the box change, and why did its largest effects take a decade to appear?



10 minutes · Individual · Notes permitted


Commit to one causal explanation before we investigate the system.


Timing: 3-13. Want a named cost or capability, not “shipping got cheaper.” Do not resolve.

title: Shipping Containers and Global Supply Chains
section: Interrogate the explanations
text:
Interrogate the explanations

What changed immediately when cargo entered a box?


What changed only after the surrounding system was rebuilt?


Timing: 13-17. Take four or five answers onto the board unsorted. Then reveal the second question and work down the list. Leave the board standing for the return at the end.

title: Shipping Containers and Global Supply Chains
section: Cargo crossed the port one piece at a time
text:
Cargo crossed the port one piece at a time




Each handoff consumed labor and time, exposed cargo to loss, and required another organization to coordinate.

The port was the expensive break in the journey.



Breakbulk loading, Brooklyn, 1967 · Library of Congress


Timing: 17-20. Ask what costs are visible in the photograph.

title: Shipping Containers and Global Supply Chains
section: In the chapter example, ports were nearly half the cost
text:
In the chapter example, ports were nearly half the cost


A dozen vendors moved one truckload of medicine from Chicago to France circa 1960. The two ports alone cost $1,163 of the $2,386 total.


Levinson, The Box, Chapter 1, Table 1


Timing: 20-24. Table 1: total $2,386. Ports $1,163 (48.7%). Ocean $581 (24.4%). Inland 22.9% combined. One estimated shipment, not an average.

title: Shipping Containers and Global Supply Chains
section: Before containerization, freight could rival trade barriers
text:
Before containerization, freight could rival trade barriers

In 1961, U.S. exporters spent about 12 cents of every export dollar on ocean freight.




12%


ocean freight as a share of U.S. export value



7%


average U.S. import tariff



Moving goods across oceans could cost more than the formal tariff barrier.


Timing: 24-27. These are scale comparisons rather than identical measures: freight is reported against export value, while the tariff is the average duty on imports. Levinson also notes that freight added 13% to steel pipe shipped from New York to Brazil and $20 to a refrigerator shipped from London to Cape Town.

title: Shipping Containers and Global Supply Chains
section: Fifty-eight boxes sailed from Newark in 1956
text:
Fifty-eight boxes sailed from Newark in 1956




Separated the container from the truck chassis and designed a continuous handoff among truck, ship, and rail.


Ideal-X, 1956 · Maersk/SeaLand


Timing: 27-31. April 26, 1956. Newark to Houston. McLean was a trucker.

title: Shipping Containers and Global Supply Chains
section: One fitting made different networks compatible
text:
One fitting made different networks compatible





A standard corner casting lets cranes, chassis, rail cars, and ships handle the same box.

Compatibility required common standards for dimensions, fittings, strength, identification, and operating rules.
The corner fitting itself is standardized under ISO 1161.


ArnoldReinhold / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0


Timing: 31-34. ISO/TC 104 formed 1961. ISO R668 on dimensions accepted 1968. Neither date is in Levinson.

title: Shipping Containers and Global Supply Chains
section: ISO: who sets international standards?
text:
ISO: who sets international standards?


What?
An independent, nongovernmental organization whose members are national standards bodies.
Where?
Its Central Secretariat is in Geneva, Switzerland.
When?
ISO was founded in 1947. Its freight-container committee, TC 104, was created in 1961.
Why?
Common voluntary standards let firms and countries build compatible products and infrastructure without a single company controlling the system.




Relevant here: ISO/R 668:1968 established the core classification, dimensions, and ratings for Series 1 freight containers.


ISO · Geneva headquarters · ISO/R 668:1968


Timing: 34-38. ISO officially came into existence in 1947 to coordinate and unify standards developed by national standards bodies. It remains an independent, nongovernmental organization, with a Central Secretariat in Geneva. TC 104 was created in 1961 for freight containers. ISO/R 668:1968 was the first published version of the standard that evolved into today’s ISO 668, covering Series 1 freight-container classification, dimensions, and ratings. The IB point is interoperability: once firms could rely on common dimensions and ratings, they could invest in compatible ships, cranes, rail cars, chassis, and terminals.

title: Shipping Containers and Global Supply Chains
section: A container port operates like a factory
text:
A container port operates like a factory



Panama · Course photograph


Timing: 34-38. 1,400-foot ship, 9,000 forty-foot boxes, crew of 20. Cranes move 30 to 40 boxes an hour. Ship gone in 24 hours.

title: Shipping Containers and Global Supply Chains
section: The box reduced five costs at once
text:
The box reduced five costs at once


Containerization lowered total landed cost by reducing handling, delay, risk, and coordination costs as well as freight charges.


Timing: 38-42. The just-in-time claim is Levinson’s strongest and is asserted rather than shown. A group contests it in the exercise.

title: Shipping Containers and Global Supply Chains
section: Malaysia to Cincinnati in 28 days, unopened
text:
Malaysia to Cincinnati in 28 days, unopened


Economists: it is now better to assume that moving goods is essentially costless than to assume it is an important component of production.


Timing: 42-45. 9,000 miles to Los Angeles in 23 days, 11,000 miles and 28 days door to door, under the price of one business-class ticket.

title: Shipping Containers and Global Supply Chains
section: Why the payoff took a decade
text:
Why the payoff took a decade


The payoff waited for standards, infrastructure, organizational redesign, and agreements over dock labor, port investment, and regulation.


Edison had the incandescent bulb by 1879. Twenty years later, 3 percent of American homes had electric light.



Edison lamp · Smithsonian Institution


Timing: 45-51. “Political bargains” means concrete agreements over who bore the costs of transition: union work rules and compensation for dock labor, public and private investment in new terminals, and regulatory approval for new shipping practices. Ask who could organize against the change. Dockworkers, ship lines, and incumbent ports had concentrated losses.

title: Shipping Containers and Global Supply Chains
section: Ricardo’s model assumed away shipping costs
text:
Ricardo’s model assumed away shipping costs





Ricardo’s 1817 wine-and-cloth example compared production costs in England and Portugal. Moving the goods between them cost nothing in the model.


Comparative advantage explains why specialization can create gains. Transport costs help determine whether specialization across distance is viable.



David Ricardo, c. 1821 · Thomas Phillips / National Portrait Gallery


Timing: 51-54. A qualification, not a refutation. Ricardo intentionally abstracted from transport costs. Modern economic geography puts distance, transport costs, and location closer to the center of the analysis.

title: Shipping Containers and Global Supply Chains
section: Multinational plants became one production network
text:
Multinational plants became one production network


Firms could reorganize production across viable locations as wages, exchange rates, capabilities, and other conditions changed.


Timing: 57-61. Distinguish a multinational, which owns plants in several countries, from a network, in which each plant specializes and they exchange components.

title: Shipping Containers and Global Supply Chains
section: Fragmented production created two core IB decisions
text:
Fragmented production created two core IB decisions


Where?
Where should each activity take place?
Wages · skills · infrastructure · market access · risk

Who?
Who should perform it?
The firm itself · an outside supplier


Lower trade costs expanded the set of viable locations and suppliers. We will study this later in the semester.


Timing: 61-63. This is the bridge to the standard IB questions of location, offshoring, outsourcing, and ownership. Keep it brief here; those choices return later in the course.

title: Shipping Containers and Global Supply Chains
section: Trade surged, but causation remains difficult
text:
Trade surged, but causation remains difficult



2×


manufactured trade grew more than twice as fast as manufacturing output in the decade after 1966


What else changed?
Tariffs · exchange rates · oil shocks · computers

How could we isolate the container’s effect?



Propose a comparison that could separate the container from the other changes.


Timing: 63-68. Manufactured trade grew 2x manufacturing output and 2.5x global output in the decade after 1966. Push for research designs, not for more data: a constant shipment priced over time, similar routes containerized at different dates, trade around port conversion.

title: Shipping Containers and Global Supply Chains
section: The same people gained as consumers and faced new competition at work
text:
The same people gained as consumers and faced new competition at work


As consumers
4× more imported product varieties in the United States, 2002 vs. 1972
Estimated gain from added variety: nearly 3% of GDP

At work
Export hubs gained jobs and investment.
Import-competing workers faced more distant competitors.


France: some manufacturers shifted production abroad rather than absorb the cost of a shorter workweek with unchanged pay.



Consumer gains were broad. Employment losses were concentrated in particular occupations and places.


Timing: 66-70. Individuals occupy both roles: consumers and workers. Four times the imported varieties by 2002 against 1972; estimated benefit near 3 percent of GDP. Keep the France example as an illustration of firms gaining a credible relocation option.

title: Shipping Containers and Global Supply Chains
section: Containerization relocated the port economy
text:
Containerization relocated the port economy




Port Newark, 1996 · SCI Archives



New York’s finger piers lacked the contiguous land and surface connections container terminals required.

Port activity shifted to large terminals at Newark and Elizabeth, New Jersey, just west of New York City. Waterfront employment and investment moved with it.


Timing: 70-74. Elizabeth is in northeastern New Jersey, immediately south of Newark, and forms part of the Port Newark-Elizabeth Marine Terminal complex. The regional port survived; activity moved from Manhattan and Brooklyn piers to larger New Jersey terminals. Liverpool declined. Busan, Seattle, Felixstowe, and Tanjung Pelepas rose.

title: Shipping Containers and Global Supply Chains
section: What still resists distance?
text:
What still resists distance?
Running shoes · fresh flowers · cars · cement · accounting software · haircuts

Rank them from easiest to hardest to serve from 5,000 miles away. For each, name the transport or coordination cost that drives your ranking.


Value-to-weight, perishability, transport mode, and the need for face-to-face delivery still shape what can be traded over distance.


Timing: 74-80. Volunteers only. Use the examples to separate different physical frictions. Running shoes travel well in containers. Fresh flowers rely on air freight and cold chains. Cars use roll-on, roll-off vessels. Cement is heavy and low-value relative to weight. Accounting software moves digitally. Haircuts require co-location.

title: Shipping Containers and Global Supply Chains
section: Cheap freight did not erase location
text:
Cheap freight did not erase location


Containerization changed
Handling · inventory · reliability · coordination

Border frictions still divide markets
Currencies · jurisdictions · trade rules · political risk


Why do firms keep production in high-wage locations?


Timing: 80-83. Define border frictions here for the first time: costs created by crossing national boundaries rather than by physical distance itself. Two or three rapid answers on the closing question. Tomorrow begins with currencies.

title: Shipping Containers and Global Supply Chains
section: 1985 without containerization
text:
1985 without containerization

Cargo still crosses ports piece by piece. Jet travel, computers, oil shocks, and tariff reductions are unchanged.




Japanese cars in the United States
Walmart
Shenzhen manufacturing
Toyota just-in-time production



New York garment district decline
Nespresso capsule
Bangalore software services
Kenyan cut flowers



10 minutes · Groups of four
Without containerization, is your example mostly unchanged · later/smaller · unlikely in this form?
Name one mechanism that explains your choice.


Timing: 85-101. Assign one case per group. Likely mostly unchanged: Japanese cars, Toyota JIT, Bangalore software, Kenyan flowers. Likely later/smaller: Walmart, New York garments, Nespresso. Shenzhen may generate a useful argument between later/smaller and unlikely in this form. Traps: cars cross on roll-on, roll-off vessels; Toyota developed JIT before containerization; Bangalore depends on telecommunications; Kenyan flowers move by air. Push students to name the mechanism linking containerization to the outcome.

title: Shipping Containers and Global Supply Chains
section: Reflection: return to your IB Voice
text:
Reflection: return to your IB Voice

What exactly did the box change, and why did its largest effects take a decade to appear?


Revise your opening answer. Which link in your causal argument changed?


Standards, complementary investment, organizational change, and policy lowered total landed cost. Global competition and fragmented production followed.


Tomorrow: one production network, many currencies.


Timing: 106-108. Mark one sentence in the opening response and write a revised version beneath it.
